body: Eleven minutes after saying goodnight, two men are still standing between their cars in a chapel car park in the rain, at twenty to ten on a Tuesday. One of them has had his keys in his hand for most of those eleven minutes. He has been carrying a sentence around for three weeks and he says it badly, at the exact moment the other man reaches for his door handle: that he has noticed the way he talks about his wife when she is not in the room, and that it has got worse since the spring. Then neither of them says anything. The rain keeps going. Eventually one of them says right, well, and gets in.

That was the verse. Not the mug and not the slogan on the men’s breakfast flyer — that damp, badly timed sentence in a car park, and the eleven minutes of failing to say it first, is the whole of what the proverb is describing.
Iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another. It is quoted constantly, and almost always as encouragement, which is a strange use for it, because the image is not an encouraging one.

Take the picture literally, because it repays the attention. Sharpening is not two pieces of metal agreeing with each other. It is abrasion. There has to be contact, real pressure, and a consistent angle held over many passes. There is a noise while it is happening. There is swarf on the floor afterwards, and the blade that comes off the stone is smaller than the blade that went on — it gets sharper by getting less. None of that is comfortable for either party, and none of it can be done by two objects that are in the same building and never touch.

That assumption sits underneath this band as well. Every station on it is hosted rather than merely automated, 12 Inspire Family voices between them, and a host is somebody who is in the room often enough to be recognised. That is a different arrangement from a feed, and it costs more to run.

Doing the thing properly is expensive, which is most of the reason so little of it happens. To be sharpened you have to be within reach of somebody who has the standing to say the hard sentence; you have to have given them that standing in advance, before you knew what they would use it for; and you have to stay in the room afterwards while it is awkward. Every part of that costs hours you would rather spend somewhere easier. Sharpening makes a noise, removes material, and cannot be done at a distance. Most of what men call friendship is none of those.

Men have not stopped having friends. They have stopped having friendships with a fixed location. The people a man is closest to are now spread across three cities and a group chat, and the contact between them is asynchronous, elective and lightly edited before sending. He is loved. He is also, in any given ordinary week, unobserved. Nobody sees the tone he uses at half past six on a Thursday, so nobody can mention it, and a man cannot be corrected by people who only ever meet the summary he files of himself.

The dial is arranged around the opposite property. A station holds one frequency permanently, no two stations share a number, and the schedule is published before it airs rather than rearranged around whoever happens to be listening. Nothing here moves to a better slot overnight. That fixity is what makes returning possible, and returning is what makes recognition possible: the reason people who grew up with radio can put a hand on a frequency in the dark is that it was in the same place every time they reached.
There is a substitute on the market, and it deserves naming, because a great many men have bought it in good faith.

Call it accountability as a product: the app with the weekly check-in question, the paid coach, the small group with a curriculum and a workbook and a fixed number of weeks. It is better than nothing and it is not a scam. Men do genuinely surface things there that they had never said out loud. What the format cannot manufacture is standing. The question is asked by somebody with no stake in the answer, on a schedule that ends in March, and the answer can be adjusted a little without anybody being any the wiser. A relationship you can leave at no cost cannot press hard enough to remove material. It can only ever polish.
Two pieces of iron. One piece and a slogan sharpens nothing.

A man of sixty-odd and a man of twenty-six have been rebuilding the same motorbike in a garage on the edge of an industrial estate on Saturday mornings for six years. Mostly they do not talk. The radio is on and neither of them chose what is playing. The older one makes tea in the same two mugs and has never once used the word accountability in his life. On a Saturday in October, without looking up from the carburettor he is cleaning, he says nine words about the way the younger man has been speaking to his mother. The younger man says nothing and goes on holding the torch. They finish at one, as usual. He speaks to his mother differently after that.

The nine words worked because of the six years. Nothing in those six years looked like sharpening while it was happening — it was tea, and a carburettor, and the same two mugs. That was the standing being accumulated, and there is no way to acquire it in advance of needing it.

The cost is real and it should be said plainly. A man who has told you the truth is harder to be around for a while afterwards, and you will find yourself managing the friendship for a month. You will also lose people this way, because some friendships turn out not to be load-bearing and only discover it the first time weight is put on them. And you will sometimes simply be wrong: you will say the careful thing and find you had misread the whole situation, and there is no method for knowing which kind of Tuesday you are having beforehand.

But the friction is not a defect in the friendship. It is the friendship. A relationship that has never cost either party anything has never been asked to carry anything, and it will not be there in the year that needs carrying. The noise is not a sign that something has gone wrong; the noise is the evidence that contact is being made. Silence between two men who see each other constantly is not peace. Very often it is just distance, arranged comfortably.

So the proverb is not encouragement and it never was. It is a specification, and a demanding one: two pieces, real contact, a held angle, repeated passes, over years, with material coming off both. Quoting it at a man who has no such friendship does not give him one. It only tells him what he is missing, in a tone that suggests he ought to have it already.
All of which is theory until Saturday. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air and playing right now. What is on them comes in four kinds. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, gospel, country, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. Every one of them holds its number permanently, which means it can be returned to.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 315.20 — Corner Cipher. A cipher is precisely the arrangement this article has been describing, and it existed on street corners long before anybody made a discipleship programme out of it: men standing in a circle taking turns, everybody hearing exactly what everybody else brought, nobody able to hide behind an arrangement, and the standard set by whoever happens to be stood next to you rather than by a chart. It is Christian rap out of Atlanta with Marcus Reed on the mic, trap and lyrical and soul-gospel, and the show is called The Corner because he is talking about the block he actually came from rather than a block in general. That specificity is the whole point. It is the sound of men who got sharp by staying in range of each other.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually own. Add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band finds out which frequencies people are really reaching for, which is how the next station gets built and how the ones already on air get better.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 315.20 on in the garage on Saturday and let it run. Then do the harder half, which no station can do for you: ring the man who has known you longest, put a fixed hour in the week where neither of you has to keep choosing it, and keep turning up to it for a year until he has seen enough of your ordinary weeks to be able to say the sentence. It will make a noise when he does. That is how you will know it was iron.
